§0Part 1 · cells

What is a cell?

Wildly different on the outside, strikingly similar within.

The cell theory states that all living things are built from the same basic units — cells. A cell is a self-contained, membrane-bound structure that can carry out the basic functions of life. Understand the cell and you understand most of what a body does.

Label Key — what you're looking at
The point
Bacteria, blood cells, plant cells, neurons, diatoms, epithelium — utterly different shapes and sizes, yet all are cells running the same chemistry with the same kinds of molecules.

The features every cell shares

  • A boundary membrane — separates inside from outside; studded with pumps, carriers & channels to control what enters and leaves.
  • Genetic information — stored as nucleic acid (usually DNA); the flow is DNA → RNA → protein.
  • Energy currency — all cells obtain energy and spend it as ATP.
  • Ribosomes — the machines that build proteins.
  • A common ancestor — every cell descends from one ancestral cell (self-replication).
  • They're dynamic — they respond to chemical, electrical & hormonal signals.
Reasoning · why "different outside, same inside"?

Because every cell descends from a common ancestor, they inherited the same core toolkit — membrane, DNA-based information, ribosomes, ATP. Shape then diverged to suit each job (a neuron stretches to signal; a red cell flattens to carry oxygen), but the internal machinery stayed conserved. Shared ancestry explains the shared interior.

§1Part 2 · the great divide

Prokaryotes vs Eukaryotes

One line splits all cellular life: is the DNA boxed in a nucleus, or not?

All cellular life falls into two groups. Prokaryotes (pro- = "before", karyon = "nucleus") have no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles — their DNA sits loose in the cytoplasm. Eukaryotes (eu- = "true") keep their DNA inside a proper nucleus and are packed with organelles.

Label Key — three domains, two cell types
Bacteria
Prokaryotic. The familiar microbes (E. coli, cyanobacteria…).
Archaea
Prokaryotic. A separate domain — many live in extreme environments.
Eucarya
Eukaryotic. Animals, fungi, plants & protists — everything with a nucleus.
Memory hook · pro vs eu

Prokaryote = "pro = before" the nucleus → no nucleus. Eukaryote = "eu = true" nucleus → DNA boxed away. Two of the three domains (Bacteria + Archaea) are prokaryotic; only Eucarya is eukaryotic.

§1.1The prokaryotic cell

Small, simple, and fast-dividing (by binary fission). Everything — DNA, proteins, ribosomes — shares one cytoplasmic compartment.

Label Key — decoded
Nucleoid
The central region where the DNA is bundled — not membrane-bound (no true nucleus).
Ribosomes
Scattered in the cytoplasm — protein synthesis (present in all cells).
Cell wall
Rigid, of peptidoglycan — gives shape & protection.
Cell (plasma) membrane
The boundary separating cell from environment.
Periplasmic space
The gap between inner membrane and cell wall / outer membrane.
Pili & flagella
Pili = attachment + DNA transfer; flagella = tail-like structures for movement.

§1.2The eukaryotic cell — the master map

Large and complex, dividing by mitosis / meiosis. This one figure names nearly every structure the rest of the guide unpacks — treat it as your map.

Label Key — the organelle roll-call
Nucleus + nucleolus
Holds the chromosomes & DNA; the nucleolus builds ribosomes (§2.3).
Cell membrane
The outer boundary (§2.1).
Rough & smooth ER
Membrane factory — granular (with ribosomes) & agranular (§2.4).
Golgi apparatus
Sorting & packaging depot (§2.5).
Mitochondrion
ATP powerhouse (§2.7).
Lysosome
Digestive vesicle (§2.6).
Ribosomes
Protein synthesis — free or ER-bound.
Cytoskeleton
Microtubules & microfilaments — the internal scaffold (§2.2).
Centrioles
Organise cell division (§2.8).
Glycogen & granules
Stored fuel & secretory cargo in the cytoplasm.
Prokaryote vs eukaryote — the comparison
FeatureProkaryoteEukaryote
Cell sizeSmallLarge
OrganisationSimple (no nucleus/organelles)Complex (nucleus + organelles)
DNA locationFree in cytoplasm (nucleoid)Enclosed in a nucleus
ReproductionBinary fissionMitosis / meiosis
Membrane organellesAbsentPresent
ExamplesBacteria, ArchaeaAnimals, plants, fungi, protists
§2Part 3 · the eukaryotic organelles

The eukaryotic cell, organelle by organelle

Each compartment is a specialised workshop. Here's what each one is, does, and why it's built the way it is.

You should be able to recognise and describe the location and function of each organelle. Here's the whole cell mapped, then each part in turn.

Label Key
Everything at once
Centrioles · secretory granules · nucleus (chromosomes/DNA, nucleolus) · Golgi · cell membrane · mitochondria · rough & smooth ER · ribosomes · lysosome · glycogen · microfilaments. Each is decoded below.

§2.1The cell membrane

The interface between the cell and its world — a phospholipid bilayer studded with cholesterol and proteins.

Label Key
Lipid bilayer (~5 nm)
A double sheet of phospholipids — the "double-layered film" seen in the EM (A) and modelled in (B).
Phospholipid
A hydrophilic (water-loving) head + two hydrophobic (water-repelling) tails. Tails point inward (away from water), heads face out — forming the two surfaces of the bilayer.
Protein molecule
Embedded proteins: transmembrane receptors (convert outside signals to inside effects), channels/carriers (let specific molecules through), and adhesion proteins (bind cells together / to matrix).
Reasoning · why a bilayer forms

Each phospholipid is amphipathic — one end loves water, the other hates it. Drop many into water and they spontaneously arrange so the water-hating tails hide together in the middle and the water-loving heads face the watery inside and outside. That self-assembly gives a stable, self-sealing barrier — and it's why the membrane is a fluid mosaic: the lipids and proteins can drift sideways.

§2.2Cytoplasm & cytoskeleton

The cytoplasm is everything enclosed by the membrane except the nucleus — the organelles plus the cytosol (the jelly-like fluid). Running through it is the cytoskeleton, the cell's scaffolding and transport network.

Label Key — three filament types
Microfilaments
Actin (shown blue in the micrograph). Thinnest; drive cell shape & muscle contraction.
Intermediate filaments
(red). Rope-like; give mechanical strength.
Microtubules
(green). Thickest; act as tracks for motor proteins to haul organelles, and build the spindle in cell division.
Reasoning · a skeleton that moves

Unlike your bony skeleton, the cytoskeleton constantly builds and dismantles itself. That lets one system do many jobs: hold the cell's shape, form internal "roads" for transporting cargo, pull the cell along, and physically drag chromosomes apart during division.

§2.3Nucleus & ribosomes

The nucleus is the control centre — it houses the DNA and directs the cell's activities.

Label Key
Nuclear envelope
A double membrane (inner + outer). The outer membrane is continuous with the ER.
Nuclear pores
Gateways bridging both membranes — all traffic in/out of the nucleus passes through them.
Nuclear lamina
A mesh of intermediate filaments just inside the inner membrane — structural support.
Chromatin
DNA + proteins. Heterochromatin = tightly packed (silent); euchromatin = loose (active).
Nucleolus
The dense spot where ribosomes are assembled.
Ribosomes
Build proteins — found free in the cytoplasm and bound to the rough ER.
Memory hook · nucleolus vs nucleus

Nucleolus makes ribosomes (both have the "o"); the nucleus is the whole control room around it. And note: like the mitochondrion, the nucleus has a double membrane — see §2.7.

§2.4Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)

A vast network of membranous tubes continuous with the nuclear envelope — the cell's synthesis and transport highway. It comes in two forms.

Label Key
Rough ER
Studded with ribosomes (that's the "rough"). Synthesises & folds proteins destined for the membrane, secretion, or lysosomes; proteins collect in the cisternal space (lumen) and pinch off in vesicles.
Smooth ER
No ribosomes. Site of lipid & steroid synthesis, detoxification, and calcium storage.
Cisternal space / lumen
The interior where finished proteins are held before shipping.
Memory hook · rough vs smooth

Rough = Ribosomes = pRoteins. Smooth = no ribosomes = lipidS & Steroids (and detox). If it makes protein it's rough; if it makes fat it's smooth.

§2.5Golgi apparatus

The cell's post office: it receives products from the ER, modifies and labels them, then sorts and ships them to their destinations.

Label Key
Cisternae
The stack of flattened membrane sacs that make up the Golgi.
Cis face (receiving)
Faces the ER — incoming vesicles fuse here.
Trans face (shipping)
The outgoing side — processed products leave in vesicles bound for lysosomes or the membrane.
Transport vesicles
Bud from the ER → Golgi, and from the Golgi → their targets.
Reasoning · why a stack with two faces?

Products move through the cisternae like an assembly line, getting modified (e.g. sugar chains added) step by step. Keeping a distinct receiving (cis) side and shipping (trans) side gives direction to the flow — raw material in one end, finished, addressed parcels out the other.

§2.6Vesicles, endosomes, lysosomes & peroxisomes

A transport-and-disposal network that originates from the trans-Golgi and moves material into, out of, and around the cell.

Label Key — the routes
Endocytosis
The membrane engulfs material to bring it in (uptake). Exocytosis is the reverse — secreting material out.
Phagocytosis
"Cell eating" — engulfing large particles (e.g. bacteria) into a vesicle.
Endosomes
Sorting vesicles (early → late) that receive endocytosed cargo.
Lysosome
Membrane-bound sac of hydrolytic (digestive) enzymes at acidic pH ~4.5–5.0. Breaks down engulfed material and worn-out organelles.
Autophagy
"Self-eating" — the cell digests its own damaged organelles via an autophagosome that fuses with a lysosome.
Peroxisome
(related organelle) Contains enzymes for oxidation reactions; makes and then destroys hydrogen peroxide (via catalase) and breaks down fatty acids.
Real-world · why the acid & the membrane matter

Lysosomal enzymes only work at acidic pH, so if they leaked into the neutral cytosol they'd do little harm — a built-in safety catch. When lysosomes can't break something down (a missing enzyme), undigested material piles up — the basis of lysosomal storage diseases.

§2.7Mitochondria

The powerhouse of the cell — it generates most of the cell's ATP by cellular respiration, using oxygen.

Label Key
Outer membrane
Smooth; the outer boundary.
Inner membrane
Thrown into folds called cristae — this folding packs in huge surface area for the ATP-generating machinery.
Cristae
The inner-membrane folds themselves.
Matrix
The inner space, filled with soluble enzymes of respiration (and the mitochondrion's own DNA).
Intermembrane space
The gap between the two membranes.
Reasoning · why fold the inner membrane?

ATP is generated on the inner membrane, so more membrane = more ATP. Folding it into cristae crams an enormous surface area into a tiny organelle — the same trick as the nasal conchae or intestinal villi: when a job happens on a surface, wrinkle the surface to do more of it.

§2.8Centrosomes & centrioles

The cell's microtubule-organising centre — it marshals the cytoskeleton and runs cell division.

Label Key
Centrosome
The microtubule-organising centre (MTOC) — made mainly of protein tubulin; it regulates cell division.
A pair of centrioles
Two barrel-shaped structures inside the centrosome, set at right angles.
Microtubules
Radiate out from the centrosome; in division they form the spindle apparatus that separates chromosomes.
Reasoning · why it matters at division

Before a cell divides, the centrosome duplicates and the two copies move to opposite poles. From there they grow the spindle — the microtubule ropes that grab chromosomes and haul one full set to each daughter cell. Get this wrong and daughter cells inherit the wrong number of chromosomes.

§2.R Recall checklist — the organelles
  • Membrane — phospholipid bilayer (hydrophilic heads out, hydrophobic tails in) + proteins; fluid mosaic.
  • Cytoskeleton — microfilaments (actin) · intermediate filaments · microtubules (tracks + spindle).
  • Nucleus — double membrane + pores; chromatin (hetero/eu); nucleolus makes ribosomes.
  • ER — Rough = Ribosomes = pRoteins; Smooth = lipids/steroids + detox.
  • Golgi — modify, sort, ship; cis (receive, from ER) → trans (ship).
  • Lysosome — acidic (pH ~4.5–5) digestive enzymes; autophagy. Peroxisome — oxidation, catalase, H₂O₂.
  • Mitochondrion — double membrane, inner folded into cristae; makes ATP.
  • Centrosome — MTOC + pair of centrioles; builds the mitotic spindle.
